strengths: Addresses a genuine and underserved gap: MCIF is among the first benchmarks to jointly cover three modalities (text, speech, video), four typologically diverse languages, both short- and long-form context, and 13 diverse tasks spanning recognition, translation, QA, and summarization within a unified instruction-following framework.

Strong data curation methodology: professional linguists/translators were hired with documented guidelines, cost details, and a secondary verification step (translators reviewing source content), which lends credibility to annotation quality relative to many automatically-constructed benchmarks.

Thoughtful QA design that explicitly labels answerability and required input modality (A/V/AV/NA) and balances general, abstract-based, and transcript-based questions, enabling fine-grained analysis of modality dependence.
Careful attention to data contamination by selecting the most recent available ACL conference talks at collection time.
Broad and relevant baseline coverage (21 models across LLM/SpeechLLM/VideoLLM/MLLM categories) with detailed reproducibility information (HF versions, model links, generation settings).
The Fix/Mix prompt design is a nice contribution for probing robustness to instruction paraphrasing, and the reported degradation from Fix to Mix is a genuinely interesting empirical finding.
Permissive CC-BY 4.0 license supports open research and reuse.
weaknesses: The manuscript is explicitly incomplete: it contains an in-text warning ('This section contains intermediate and incomplete results'), and Sections 5.2 (Effect of Modalities Integration) and 5.3 (Breakdown on Question Answering) are literally marked 'Work in progress...'. Additional paragraphs (e.g., 'Summarization', 'Open/Closed Models') appear as placeholder headers with hourglass icons and no content. This is a fundamental readiness issue for a paper under review at a top venue.

The benchmark's overall scale is quite small: only 21 talks (~2 hours) for the primary tasks and 220 total QA pairs split across 4 languages, 13 tasks, and multiple sub-categories (general/abstract/transcript, A/V/AV/NA). This raises concerns about the statistical reliability of fine-grained comparisons across models and languages.

Despite being framed as a 'crosslingual' benchmark, all source audio/video content is in English only; multilinguality is achieved solely through human translation of transcripts/summaries/QA into the target languages, and the source side is never non-English. This is a narrower notion of crosslinguality than the framing and title imply.

Language coverage is limited to 4 languages, explicitly justified partly by 'budget constraints,' which undercuts the paper's claim to comprehensively assess multilingual capability relative to benchmarks covering many more languages.

Only open-weight models <20B parameters are evaluated; no proprietary/closed frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude) are included, limiting insight into current SOTA capability, and the planned 'Open vs Closed Models' comparison is itself unfinished.

Evaluation relies solely on automatic metrics (WER, COMET, BERTScore) without any human evaluation of model outputs, which is a notable gap for a benchmark whose main selling point is human-annotated gold data and open-ended QA/summarization where automatic metrics are known to correlate imperfectly with quality.

QA pairs were created and verified by 16 annotators who are 'all students and authors of this paper,' raising concerns about independence and potential bias in the annotation process, despite reasonable safeguards (guidelines, distribution targets).

The results section is largely descriptive (walking through tables) without deeper error analysis, statistical significance testing, or synthesis of higher-level insights beyond surface-level trends already visible in the tables.

Given the missing analyses, it's not currently possible to fully evaluate central claimed contributions such as the 'multifaceted evaluation' across modality integration and QA breakdowns, since these sections are unwritten.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated benchmark combining multilinguality (4 languages), multimodality (text, speech, video), long- and short-form context, and 13 tasks in a single unified resource — filling a real gap identified in the related work survey.

Data curation is relatively rigorous: professional linguists/translators for transcription and translation, 16 expert annotators for QA pairs with a structured distribution (general/transcript/abstract questions) and explicit modality-requirement labeling (A/V/AV/NA), plus care taken to avoid data contamination by using recent ACL 2023 talks.
Broad evaluation effort covering 21 open-weight models across four model families (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs), with two prompt variants (fix/mix) to probe robustness to instruction phrasing.
The related-work section is thorough and clearly positions the contribution relative to existing speech-text and vision-text benchmarks.
License (CC-BY 4.0) and intended open release support reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly unfinished: Section 5 is flagged with 'WARNING! This section contains intermediate and incomplete results', Sections 5.2 and 5.3 simply state 'Work in progress...', and subsections such as 'Open vs Closed Models' and parts of the Summarization discussion are empty or placeholder text (e.g., stray icons left in text). This alone makes the submission not evaluable as a complete scientific contribution.

Core resource statistics are very small in absolute terms: only 21 talks (2 hours of video) form the core benchmark, with 100 samples (~10 hours) only for summarization; this is a very small-scale benchmark for the many claims of comprehensiveness, raising concerns about statistical reliability of the reported scores (especially per-language, per-task breakdowns with likely very few examples each).

QA annotation was performed by the paper's own students/co-authors rather than independent/professional annotators, which is a weaker form of 'human annotation' than claimed, and raises concerns about potential bias and limited inter-annotator agreement reporting (no IAA statistics given).
Appendix B.1 contains broken/missing hyperlinks for guidelines ('available at: )'), suggesting incomplete appendix preparation and reproducibility documentation.

Language coverage (German, Italian, Chinese) is small and admittedly chosen partly due to budget constraints and availability of co-authors rather than principled typological/linguistic diversity criteria, limiting generalizability of 'crosslingual' claims.

Evaluation metrics are somewhat coarse: WER, COMET, and (rescaled) BERTScore are used uniformly across very heterogeneous open-ended QA/summarization tasks; no human evaluation or correlation study is provided to validate that these automatic metrics adequately capture answer quality in this crosslingual, multimodal, long-context setting.

Only models under 20B parameters are evaluated, excluding larger open and closed (proprietary) models; the 'Open vs Closed Models' comparison teased in the text is entirely missing, leaving an important comparison axis unaddressed.

The analysis in Section 5.1 is somewhat superficial/descriptive (listing numbers per model) without deeper statistical analysis, significance testing, or error analysis beyond a few anecdotal examples (e.g., Ola captioning slides instead of transcribing).

Given the incomplete state of the results and analysis sections, it is not possible to properly assess the paper's central empirical claims and contributions, which is a serious submission/soundness issue for a venue review.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: no existing benchmark jointly covers speech, vision, and text modalities, crosslingual instruction-following, and both short- and long-form contexts with human annotations.

Substantial manual curation effort: professional transcription/translation across 4 languages, 220 expert-created and verified QA pairs with structured categorization (general/transcript/abstract-based, and modality-of-answer labels A/V/AV/NA), which enables fine-grained diagnostic analysis.

Careful attention to data contamination by using the most recent available ACL 2023 talks at collection time, and reasonable domain choice (scientific talks) that naturally provides multimodal, multilingual-relevant content.

Broad and systematic evaluation: 21 open-weight models spanning LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs, evaluated under two prompt regimes (fixed vs. mixed) to probe robustness to instruction phrasing, which is a nice methodological touch beyond typical static benchmarks.
Good reproducibility documentation in appendices (prompts, model versions, generation settings, annotation guidelines, cost details) and permissive CC-BY 4.0 release.
Interesting qualitative failure analysis (undertranslation, wrong-language defaults, refusal behavior, misinterpretation of prompts) that goes beyond pure leaderboard numbers.
weaknesses: The manuscript is explicitly incomplete: Section 5.2 (effect of modality integration) and 5.3 (QA breakdown) are marked 'Work in progress...', an 'Open vs Closed Models' paragraph is empty, and the results section carries an explicit warning that results are 'intermediate and incomplete'. This is a significant issue for evaluating the paper's core contribution and claims.

Benchmark scale is fairly small (21 talks / ~2 hours for most tasks, 100 samples for summarization, 220 unique QA pairs), which raises concerns about the statistical robustness of per-language, per-task comparisons across 21 models.
Single narrow domain (NLP conference talks from ACL) limits generalizability of findings to other multimodal/multilingual real-world scenarios.

Language selection (German, Italian, Chinese) is acknowledged to be driven partly by budget and annotator availability rather than a principled typological sampling strategy, despite claims of 'typological diversity'.

QA pairs, while expert-created, were authored by the paper's own students/authors rather than independent annotators, and no inter-annotator agreement or independent quality validation metric is reported.

Evaluation relies solely on standard automatic metrics (WER, COMET, BERTScore); for open-ended QA and summarization in an instruction-following context, these may not fully capture response quality, and no human evaluation or LLM-judge validation of model outputs is provided to corroborate automatic scores.
Dense result tables lack statistical significance testing or variance estimates, making some of the comparative claims (e.g., which model is 'best') harder to trust given the small test set size.

strengths: Novel and timely contribution: the first benchmark to jointly evaluate crosslingual, multimodal (speech+video+text) instruction following over both short- and long-form inputs, filling a clear gap identified in a thorough related-work survey.

High-quality, fully parallel human annotation: professional linguists/translators produced gold transcripts and translations in 4 languages, and expert NLP annotators created 220 structured QA pairs with modality/source labels, enabling clean ablation studies.

Extensive and well-organized experimental evaluation: 23 models spanning LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs, evaluated with a consistent unified framework and appropriate task-specific metrics (WER, COMET, BERTScore).

Thoughtful experimental design choices, such as the MCIFfix/MCIFmix contrast to measure prompt robustness, and modality-ablation analysis for MLLMs, which yield genuinely informative findings (e.g., video modality is systematically underused, long-form summarization is a universal weak point).
Careful attention to data contamination (using recent ACL 2023 talks) and strong reproducibility/transparency (released guidelines, code, model outputs, licensing details).
Fine-grained QA breakdown by question modality and source reveals nuanced, non-obvious model behavior (e.g., LLMs with transcripts alone can outperform MLLMs on AV questions).
weaknesses: Relatively small core benchmark size (21 talks, ~2 hours, ~15.5k words for most tasks; 100 talks only for summarization), which may limit statistical reliability and generalizability of the fine-grained per-language, per-modality comparisons.

Domain is restricted to ACL conference scientific talks only, which may not generalize to other multimodal crosslingual IF scenarios (e.g., everyday dialogue, lectures in other fields, non-scientific video content).

Model selection is capped at <20B parameters (aside from the single commercial exception, Gemini 2.5 Flash), excluding many current frontier open and closed models, which limits how representative the conclusions are of the true state of the art.

Reliance solely on automatic metrics (WER/COMET/BERTScore) for QA and summarization without any human evaluation of model outputs, which is a known limitation especially for open-ended generation and long-form summarization quality.

Only two professional annotators per language for transcription/translation, and no inter-annotator agreement statistics reported for the QA label assignments (A/V/AV/NA) or transcript/translation quality.

Some high-level findings (LLMs dominate translation, long-form is harder than short-form, models struggle with modality integration) are broadly expected from prior literature, somewhat limiting the novelty of insights beyond the benchmark resource itself.

Languages covered (English, German, Italian, Chinese) are all relatively high-resource, so claims about 'crosslingual' generalization do not extend to typologically diverse or low-resource languages despite being framed as a general contribution.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap by jointly covering three modalities (text, speech, video), four languages, two context lengths, and 13 tasks in a fully parallel design, which no prior benchmark achieves simultaneously.
Human-annotated construction with professional transcribers/translators and detailed, publicly released guidelines, which is more rigorous than many synthetic or repurposed benchmarks in this space.
Broad empirical coverage: 23 models spanning LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs, with useful ablations isolating the contribution of each modality and comparing fixed vs. diverse prompt phrasing.
Careful attention to data contamination by sourcing recent (2023) scientific talk videos rather than recycling existing corpora.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: released code, model outputs, prompts, and annotation guidelines under open licenses.
weaknesses: The core benchmark is very small (21 talks, ~2 hours, ~15.5k words; only 220 QA pairs across 4 languages), which is a fragile basis for the sweeping claims made about 13 tasks, 4 languages, and 2 context lengths; per-language/per-task cells likely contain very few examples, undermining statistical reliability of the fine-grained comparisons (e.g., fix vs. mix prompt sensitivity, modality ablations).

Single narrow domain (ACL conference talks) limits generalizability of conclusions to broader multimodal/crosslingual instruction-following scenarios; results may reflect idiosyncrasies of scientific-presentation register and slide-heavy video content rather than general model capability.

Model selection is restricted to <20B parameters (plus one proprietary model), excluding many current frontier open and closed multimodal systems, which limits the relevance of the benchmarking conclusions to state-of-the-art systems practitioners actually care about.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (WER, COMET, BERTScore) with no human evaluation of model outputs to validate that these metrics capture genuine instruction-following quality, which is a notable gap for a paper emphasizing human-annotated references as a key selling point.

Several reported results are degenerate (WER >100, strongly negative BERTScore) and attributed post hoc to prompt misinterpretation or formatting issues; this raises concern that some benchmark/prompt design choices may unfairly penalize certain models rather than cleanly measuring capability differences, and no systematic robustness check (e.g., multiple prompt templates with statistical testing) is provided beyond the single fix/mix contrast.
Despite the four languages being described as 'typologically diverse,' all are major, well-resourced languages, so claims about crosslingual generalization are narrower than the framing suggests.

The results section is largely a long sequence of per-model anecdotal observations rather than deeper synthesis or actionable modeling recommendations, reducing the paper's broader scientific contribution beyond the released dataset itself.

No analysis of inter-annotator agreement or quality control metrics for the QA pairs and translations beyond process description, leaving open questions about annotation consistency given the relatively small annotator pool (16 annotators for QA, 8 professionals for transcription/translation).

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and timely benchmark that is the first to jointly cover three modalities (text, speech, video), four typologically diverse languages, and both short- and long-form contexts in a fully parallel, human-annotated design — filling a clear gap identified in a thorough related-work survey.

Extensive and rigorous human annotation pipeline (professional transcribers/translators, dedicated QA annotators with structured guidelines, quality control via translation-as-verification) that lends credibility and quality to the resource, going beyond many prior benchmarks that recycle existing noisy/contaminated data.

Very broad and careful experimental evaluation: 23 models spanning LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs, with both fixed and diverse (mix) prompt sets to explicitly test robustness to instruction phrasing — a dimension largely ignored by prior work.

The task taxonomy (13 tasks across 4 macro-tasks) with explicit input/output modality and crosslinguality annotations enables fine-grained, controlled ablations (e.g., modality-contribution analysis in Section 5.2, question-type breakdown in Section 5.3) that yield genuinely informative and non-trivial findings (e.g., video modality underused even in MLLMs, summarization is uniquely hard, long-form causes under-generation).

Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed appendices on models, prompts, annotation guidelines, costs, and licensing (CC-BY 4.0 data, Apache 2.0 code), plus a thoughtful ethics statement addressing flag usage and annotator compensation.
Findings are presented with manual error analysis (not just aggregate numbers), adding interpretive depth (e.g., Ola's short-form captioning failure, Gemini's over-elaboration on short segments).
weaknesses: The benchmark is fairly small in absolute scale (21 core talks for QA/transcripts, 100 for summarization, 220 QA pairs total), which may limit statistical robustness of cross-language/cross-model comparisons, especially given the many fine-grained breakdowns reported (per-language, per-modality, per-question-type) that likely have wide variance with such limited samples.

The benchmark is drawn entirely from a single narrow domain (ACL scientific talks), which may limit generalizability of conclusions to other real-world multimodal/crosslingual instruction-following scenarios (e.g., conversational, everyday video content).

Evaluation metrics have known limitations for the tasks assessed — BERTScore for open-ended QA and summarization can be a coarse proxy for semantic correctness/factuality, and no human evaluation or correlation check with human judgments is reported to validate these automatic scores.

The translation/transcription pipeline relies on an internal, confidential ASR/MT system from the annotation agency as a starting point before human correction, which is a minor transparency/reproducibility gap despite otherwise strong documentation.

Model selection is restricted to <20B parameter open-weight models (plus one commercial model), which, combined with rapid progress in MLLMs, may limit the longevity/relevance of the specific benchmarking conclusions (though the benchmark itself remains reusable).

Some reported results show extreme variance (e.g., WER >100 or negative BERTScores) without deeper discussion of whether this stems from benchmark design artifacts (e.g., prompt format mismatches) versus genuine model limitations, which could affect the fairness of cross-model comparisons.
